reasons: The warning, stopping condition, nominal rate, and 26.1% false-positive figure exactly match the source.
The relation to sequential methods is supported by the immediately following statement that sequential methods legitimise looking early.
The source explicitly states that sequential methods legitimise looking early and lists mSPRT, GAVI, group sequential design with alpha spending, and corrected-alpha approaches.
The stated unknown correctly preserves the source’s conditional power/safety tradeoff rather than claiming one method is universally preferred.
The action accurately retains the stated minimum of one full week and the practical recommendation of two weeks.
Its rationale is supported: the source cites weekly differences in behavior and says two weeks captures a full cycle of returning visitors.
The diagnostic actions—plotting daily effects and comparing first-exposure with repeat-exposure conversion—are stated verbatim in the source.
The candidate does not invent a numerical threshold for diagnosing novelty or primacy.
The visitor-volume condition, 10–20%+ target-effect range, and preference for differentiated changes rather than tweaks all match the source.
The exclusion of tweaks is a faithful rendering of the source’s below-about-100,000-visitors/month default, not an additional prohibition.
The action accurately names the homepage, top product pages, and cart as the places to concentrate tests and retains the instruction not to test low-traffic category pages.
The candidate retains both required conditions: parallel testing is impossible and external conditions can be held constant.
Its claim also preserves the source’s qualifiers that this is best for large structural changes and should be treated as weak evidence.
The trigger and action exactly reflect the instruction to re-test any surprising large winner with a holdout before banking revenue.
It appropriately does not fabricate a definition of “surprising large.”
The source explicitly recommends qualitative research first, including session replay, surveys, and user testing, when many tests cannot be run.
The candidate preserves the stated purpose of generating stronger hypotheses.

The recommendation appears within the source’s section on low-traffic methods, but the candidate supplies no low-traffic or limited-power context and therefore presents it as an unqualified general metric policy.

The source specifically frames micro-conversions as a leading indicator because purchase or revenue may not follow; although the action includes guardrails, the candidate should make the low-traffic applicability explicit.
The source explicitly says “A/B/n and bandits: only at 3,000+ orders/month,” and the candidate preserves both the method scope and numerical threshold.
The warning accurately reproduces the source’s simulated optional-stopping procedure, posterior threshold, and approximately 80% false-positive rate.
It also preserves the source’s qualification that a fixed posterior threshold does not control frequentist error under optional stopping.

The candidate makes an observed split differing from the designed split the trigger for running the test, but that discrepancy is the condition the chi-square test is meant to detect. This creates a circular detection prerequisite.
It omits the source’s instruction to test SRM early and often.
It also omits the operational consequence that, once SRM is present, results should not be trusted until the cause is found.
The described client-side flicker condition and all three mitigations—anti-flicker snippet, synchronous high-head loading, or server-side testing—are stated in the source.
The candidate retains the material anti-flicker cost as an unknown rather than denying it.
The prerequisite concerning same-user pre-experiment data and the positive condition of returning identified users are supported.

However, the exclusion incorrectly turns a case of reduced or weaker expected variance reduction for mostly new or anonymous DTC traffic into a categorical exclusion. The source says CUPED is “not a magic fix” in that setting, not that it must not be used.
The source’s concluding recommendation is conditional on platform availability and returning identified users; those conditions can coexist with a business that has substantial new traffic.
The supplied excerpt ends after the A/B-test description in a section titled “multi-armed bandits vs A/B tests,” with no subsequent bandit-specific comparison.
The candidate correctly labels this as unresolved rather than inventing missing bandit guidance.

omissions.description: Conditional guidance for choosing group sequential testing versus always-valid inference is not represented as an actionable recommendation.
omissions.quote: Spotify's guidance: if you can estimate the expected sample size well, GST is more powerful; if you cannot, always-valid is safer.

omissions.description: The source gives adjusted reported-significance thresholds for a stated number of peeks, which no candidate represents.
omissions.quote: to get a true 5% you need reported significance of 2.9% (1 peek), 2.2% (2), 1.8% (3), 1.4% (5), 1.0% (10).

omissions.description: The source advises filtering bot traffic because it can create skew and sample-ratio mismatch; this is not represented by a candidate.
omissions.quote: Bot traffic: bots create skew and SRM; filter them (Kohavi/Sonnet).

omissions.description: The source identifies mid-test tracking breakage as invalidating an experiment; this is not represented by a candidate.
omissions.quote: Tracking breakage: if the pixel/event breaks mid-test, the experiment is invalid.

omissions.description: The source directs correction for multiple comparisons using Bonferroni or FDR; this is not represented by a candidate.
The source advises pre-registering segments to avoid post-hoc segment fishing; this is not represented by a candidate.
omissions.quote: Segment fishing: slicing results after the fact until you find a "winning" segment is p-hacking. Pre-register segments.

omissions.description: The source’s auditing rule for surprising figures is not represented by a candidate.
omissions.quote: Twyman's law: any figure that looks interesting or surprising is usually wrong.

omissions.description: The source recommends two simpler ecommerce-oriented variance-reduction choices not represented as candidate actions.
omissions.quote: Simpler cousins that help ecommerce more: pick a proportion metric instead of a raw revenue mean, and winsorize (cap) outlier orders.

source_limitations: The supplied excerpt ends mid-section 8, after the A/B-test description; it does not contain the promised bandit-specific comparison or any continuation of that section.

Several thresholds and platform-use claims are asserted with citations or vendor attributions, but the excerpt does not provide the underlying studies, data, implementation details, or definitions needed to independently assess them.

Some recommendations intentionally lack operational thresholds or decision procedures, including what qualifies as a surprising large winner, acceptable anti-flicker delay, or a novelty/primacy-effect threshold.
